paras: Image: Nintendo EPD/Nintendo via Polygon Add Polygon.com on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Sign in to your Polygon.com account follow Follow followed Followed Thread Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Speedrunners have had their hands on the Nintendo Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for a couple of days now, and some funky tricks have already been discovered. In particular, the remake's addition of a jumping mechanic has enabled new speedrunning tactics that just weren't possible in the Nintendo 64 original or its 3DS remake.

Videos from YouTubers like Kethaldo and Knightpohtayto, as well as Bluesky user Mircacle, show how actor jumping is essentially a glitched super jump that players can do with certain aimable tools in Ocarina of Time. To perform the trick, players have to find a movable object, or "actor," in the game's environments, like a chest or movable tombstone. When standing on it, players then have to shoot, press the lock-on button (ZL by default) before it's done being used, and then jump as soon as the animation ends.

By doing this, Link can jump much higher than he is supposed to. When used at certain parts of Ocarina of Time's levels, it's possible to jump even higher and skip massive swaths of the game. Right now, it's easiest to pull off when using the hookshot, so actor jumps are worth attempting once you get it.

paras: The anticipated remake of the seminal Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time dropped this week. Lifelong fans are returning to a familiar but altered Hyrule. The world originally rendered in 1998 has greater fidelity, hunkier non-playable characters, wiser chickens and, most notably, a jump button. For the regular player it’s a marvel and an adjustment. For speedrunners, it’s a tantalizing playground of tech to be discovered. As the weekend rolls out, and runners dredge the kingdom for secret exploits, they’re establishing a potential blueprint for record times. As well as uncovering some bizarre horrors along the way.

To say The Legend of Zelda series has some abnormal tech is an understatement. Ever since Link stepped out of his treehouse into a 3D, polygonal world, it was clear the code that binds his reality had a soft underbelly. Ocarina’s boomerang can rewrite item placement. Wind Waker’s camera can launch little Toon Link into hyperspeed across the ocean. Skyward Sword’s opening menu seems to exist in some kind of temporal pocket dimension. Nintendo’s fine tuned games have always operated on peculiar physics, but for speedrunners, a return to Ocarina presents an opportunity to rewrite the playbook.

The most obvious source for potential run-aiding glitches is Link’s newfound ability to jump. Like in Breath of the Wild, Link no longer needs to run off a cliff to remember how to use his knees. In standard play, Link can go higher. Speedrunners want to see just how high he can go. Find unassuming geography that can act as shortcuts. Some of the classics, like the building-bounding ‘Hookshot Jump,’ appear to be viable. One of the most popular pieces of tech revolves around open chests. Now that Link can step into them, positioning his feet inside them at just the right angle seems to bristle the game, launching the player like a trampoline. Dropping a bomb in there seems to help as well.

Had Israel been a democracy, we would have seen scenes of celebration similar to the ones we saw this year in Hungary, Brazil and Serbia, where political forces with undemocratic tendencies were defeated. But Israel is not a democracy, and Netanyahu was not necessarily defeated.

The second, more relevant way of reading the results of the Israeli election would necessitate accepting the apartheid nature of Israel and seeing the electoral arithmetic through that prism. In this case, Netanyahu won because he secured 53 seats in the Knesset – five more than the anti-Netanyahu Jewish bloc.

Floods prompted by the collapse of a melting glacier killed more than 1,500 people in Nepal and caused nearly $5 billion in damages.

pg:https://www.theguardian.com/games/202.desc: When our writer found himself among the hundreds on Oxford Street hoping to get their hands on early copies and collectibles, it was a heartwarming reminder of the shared experience of fandom
paras: It is Thursday night and I am sat blurry-eyed and runny nosed outside the Argos on Oxford Street. Incredibly, I am far from alone. This is not some strange protest against the popular retailer. When the clock strikes midnight, the lavish 4K Switch 2 remake of beloved N64 classic The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time will be released, and I have joined a lengthy queue of about 500 fans desperate to snag early copies. There are similar events taking place across the world, from Melbourne to Mexico City; at key locations, Nintendo has senior executives waiting at the tills.

These days, of course, most video games are bought as digital copies that download straight to your PC or console on the day of release. You don’t even have to get out of bed to start playing. But in a bygone era, when we used to go to shops to buy games, midnight launches offered a space for likeminded enthusiasts to gather and celebrate their fandom. Every Call of Duty, Halo or Grand Theft Auto release would have fans queueing outside branches of Game or Electronics Boutique, many dressed as favourite characters.

As one of the few Brits deluded enough to spend six hours queueing at the Wii U’s midnight launch, I have a certain fondness for the game launch as a cultural event rather than just a weird display of performative consumerism. There was something heartwarming about seeing the video game hype cycle transformed into a shared experience.

paras: Dr. Bill Frist is a heart and lung surgeon, former U.S. Senate majority leader, and Chair of the Global Board of Directors for The Nature Conservancy nonprofit. He has emerged as a prominent Republican advocate for climate action, seeking to bridge the partisan divide by emphasizing how protecting the environment benefits human health. Earlier this year, he was interviewed on stage by former Vice President Al Gore, telling the audience that climate change is the “number one force multiplier” in many public health problems.

I believe the single most important action next year is to dramatically scale new financing mechanisms already bringing billions of dollars into conservation and climate action. As The Nature Conservancy's Global Board Chair, I have watched two recently developed tools move from experiment to proof. First, Nature Bonds, which TNC helped pioneer, allow countries to refinance sovereign debt on significantly better terms and direct the savings into long-term conservation. Six projects are expected to unlock approximately $1 billion.

Second, Project Finance for Permanence (PFP) uniquely brings governments, Indigenous Peoples and local communities, philanthropy, and private capital into a single overarching agreement, tying certain funding commitments to community benefits, measurable outcomes, and accountability. Through Enduring Earth, PFPs have secured more than $2 billion in sustainable financing while supporting durable conservation across 245 million hectares.

paras: What is the single most important action you think the public, or a specific company or government, needs to take in the next year to advance the climate agenda?More governments need to stop debating carbon markets and start using them. Look at aviation: Under the United Nations’ aviation climate scheme, airlines must buy roughly 200 million carbon credits to offset the growth in their emissions through 2026. Only about 10 countries have authorized projects to sell to them. That's money meant for climate projects in developing countries, waiting on a government signature.

Voluntary buying by companies got these markets started, but it will never be big enough on its own. Singapore and Japan are great case studies. Both now put a price on carbon for their largest emitters and let them cover part of the bill with credits from projects abroad. Singapore alone has signed carbon agreements with a dozen countries. More governments should follow, both by pricing carbon at home and by authorizing projects that can sell to these buyers.

What is a climate solution that isn't getting the attention or funding it deserves?In India, more than half the nitrogen farmers spread on their fields is never taken up by the crop. Some washes into groundwater. Some escapes into the air as nitrous oxide, a gas about 270 times more potent than carbon dioxide that has driven roughly a tenth of global warming so far.

pg:https://www.theguardian.com/books/202.desc: The 81-year-old’s postapocalyptic novel The End of Everything takes home the £50,000 award
paras: Eighty-one-year-old M John Harrison has won the Booker prize for The End of Everything, a postapocalyptic novel set on a near-future Kent coast, becoming the oldest winner in the award’s history.

Gaby Wood, chief executive of the Booker Prize Foundation, said that while plenty of previous winners had dabbled in science fiction, Harrison’s was “the first Booker winner to have emerged from the bona fide SF world”. She called it “a historic win, for a writer whose decades of work are lightly worn on every page”.

Harrison, who has been publishing for six decades, overtakes Margaret Atwood, who was 79 when she shared the prize in 2019 for The Testaments. He received the £50,000 award and trophy at a ceremony in London on Monday evening.

pg:https://www.latimes.com/environment/s.desc: Democratic control of Congress changes the equation for science funding and FEMA oversight.
paras: For the weather and climate world, which has flipped between grief and rage over Trump’s science policies, the results reopen fights over funding, staffing and federal oversight. Democratic control of Congress beginning in January will give lawmakers greater power over federal spending and oversight, setting up new fights over science funding, the Federal Emergency Management Agency and the National Weather Service.
The political shift hit close to home at a Vaisala Xweather conference in South Carolina, where physician Annie Andrews had just won a Senate seat.

The most immediate fight is likely to be over money, especially for scientific research. The abuse survivors were introduced to the Pope by the local Church, and he met with them before going to the Pontifical Catholic University of Argentina in Buenos Aires to attend a meeting with representatives of social movements and the world of work.

pg:https://www.sabcnews.com/sabcnews/off.desc: The WMO raised alarm over the very strong El Niño unleashing extreme amounts of heat well into 2027
paras: The United Nations World Meteorological Organisation (WMO) has raised an alarm over the state of global climate, warning that a very strong El Niño event will unleash extreme amounts of heat and extreme weather well into 2027.

The latest WMO State of the Climate Update 2026 shows that the last 12 years have been the warmest on record, with the global average surface temperature between January and September 2026 reaching 1.47 °Celsius above the pre-industrial average.

The latest forecast from the WMO, produced by multiple partners around the world including South African Weather Services, shows an ensemble of multiple climate models predicting an overwhelming likelihood of rainfall shifts across the world, with southern Africa in particular being projected to be warmer for the November 2026-January 2027 season.

pg:https://www.theguardian.com/business/.desc: Brent crude drops below $90 and markets climb after president downplays prospect of further strikes
paras: Oil prices have fallen to the lowest level since late August while stock markets climbed higher, as markets reacted with relief to Donald Trump saying that the war on Iran is “effectively over”.

Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, fell nearly 3% to $89.66, the lowest since 31 August, on Tuesday morning, after the US president downplayed the need for military action against Iran “at this point”. The fall came after a near 6% drop on Monday on signs that the conflict might be nearing an end.
Europe’s benchmark Stoxx 600 index gained 0.9% to 662.54, hovering near a record high, which it had hit in early August on hopes for a peace deal in the Middle East.

Brent crude futures were down $2.39, or 2.58 per cent at $90.18 a barrel by 0930 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) futures fell $2.11, or 2.43 per cent to $84.74.
